device.name: OBD-II Bluetooth Adapter (ELM327 / STN)
device.notes:
The dongle every vehicle target in this repo is reached through — the transport under the transport. Bluetooth side is a serial pipe (Classic SPP/RFCOMM or BLE GATT) carrying an ASCII command set; vehicle side is OBD-II/UDS (see the `obd` block).
Because the payload is ASCII, a Bluetooth capture of a vendor app driving one of these adapters is a plain-text transcript of the vendor's diagnostic protocol. That makes this device the cheapest capture path for any OBD target.
Commands are CR-terminated; replies are complete only when the '>' prompt arrives, so a client must buffer across notifications rather than parsing each one. BLE MTU is commonly 20 bytes, so multi-notification replies are the norm, not the exception.
CONFIDENCE: GATT families A and B are cross-referenced against open-source BLE OBD clients (verification: confirmed by third-party implementations). Family C is the HM-10 pattern and is community-reported. The AT/ST command set is public documentation. No pairing, authentication or encryption is used by most BLE adapters — but not all: the family-A exemplar OBDLink CX bonds (pairing enabled for the first 5 minutes after power-on), uses a legacy pairing PIN of 123456, and always encrypts BLE communication (vendor CX adapter notes).
SAFETY: OBD pin 16 is usually unswitched — a dongle left plugged in will flatten a battery, quickly on a motorcycle. Unplug after each session.

credentials.notes: The pairing PIN is a fixed default shared across a whole product category, so it identifies nothing and protects nothing. Anyone within radio range of a plugged-in adapter can reach the vehicle bus through it — worth knowing before leaving one in the connector.
stored_on_device: Bluetooth bond with the paired host (Classic variants)

factory_reset.effect: Clears the adapter's own configuration — protocol selection, echo, headers, timeouts and any saved defaults — and returns it to power-on state. Nothing about the vehicle is touched.

procedures.indicator: The adapter re-emits its identification string.
procedures.name: ATZ software reset

steps.action: Send ATZ on the command interface.
steps.expect: Adapter resets and reports its firmware string.

steps.action: Send ATD to restore defaults if settings persist across the reset.
Unplug the adapter from the connector for a few seconds and reinsert it.
steps.notes: Also the remedy when the adapter is wedged, which cloned firmware does under multi-frame load.

methods.description: BLE variants advertise as soon as they are powered from the connector and most accept a connection with no pairing. Identify by the advertised name prefix plus one of the serial-service UUIDs. Exception: the OBDLink CX bonds (pairing window for the first 5 minutes after power-on, legacy PIN 123456) and always encrypts the link.

steps.action: Plug the adapter into the diagnostic connector and switch on the ignition.
steps.expect: Adapter LEDs light and it begins advertising.

steps.action: Scan for the advertised name prefix and a serial-service UUID, then connect.
Confirm the command interface with ATI and record the reported firmware string.
steps.expect: An ELM327 identification string. Cloned firmware reports a version it does not implement, so match the adapter_profile class rather than trusting this string.

methods.description: Bluetooth Classic (SPP/RFCOMM) variants pair with the host operating system first, using a fixed PIN. There is no button; the PIN is the proof of possession, and it is not a secret.

steps.action: Plug the adapter in and power the ignition.
Pair from the host's Bluetooth settings, entering the adapter's PIN.
steps.notes: Commonly 1234 or 0000, printed in the manual. Treat it as a default rather than a credential — it is identical across enormous numbers of dongles.

steps.action: Open the resulting serial port and confirm with ATI.

setup.notes: The adapter is the one part of an OBD-II stack that does need pairing. Bluetooth Classic variants ask for a PIN; BLE variants generally do not. Which you have is not always printed on the dongle, and the two are frequently sold under the same listing.

rejoin.notes: Pairing with a different host is just pairing again. Remove the old bond from the previous host as well — Classic adapters accept one connection at a time, and a phone reconnecting in the background is the usual cause of an adapter that "stopped working".

variants.notes: OBDLink CX (STN2310) and a large share of generic adapters. Separate notify and write characteristics. CX exception to the usual no-pairing BLE pattern: it bonds (5-minute window after power-on), legacy PIN 123456, always-encrypted link.
Vgate iCar Pro 2S BLE, LELink2. Separate notify and write characteristics.
HM-10 module clones. Single bidirectional characteristic — the same pattern as the MoTool Slacker. Community-reported.

ARM Cortex-M0, Bluetooth 4.0 (BLE), works from iOS, Android and Windows. ELM327 command-set compatible but accepts messages up to 255 bytes where a stock ELM327 stops at 8 — long diagnostic writes become one command instead of a flow-control negotiation. Protocols: ISO9141-2, KWP2000 slow and fast init, CAN 11-bit and 29-bit at 250 and 500 kbit/s, plus the BMW OEM protocols KWP2000, KWP2000*, D-CAN and UDS. Field-updatable firmware. The vendor's reference adapter for MotoScan, and named by TuneECU and BimmerCode.

STN1170 (reported). Bluetooth Classic v3.0 SPP — NO iOS support. First Bluetooth adapter to reach GM SW-CAN and Ford MS-CAN alongside the legislated protocols. Backwards compatible with the ELM327 command set plus the ST extensions.

STN2255 on original units — now out of production per the OBDLink FRPM rev F §3.1 device table; current-production MX+ uses STN2256 (reported). Dual-mode: Bluetooth Classic v3.0 with MFi (SPP/iAP2) as primary link, plus a BLE GATT pipe. MS-CAN and SW-CAN as well as every legislated protocol — the only wireless iOS adapter that reaches those manufacturer buses. Dedicated spec: device-specs/devices/obdlink-mx-plus.yaml (GATT UUIDs, button-pairing flow and firmware-update mechanism recovered from the vendor app).

RFCOMM, usually channel 1, PIN 1234 / 0000 / 6789. Names OBDII, OBDII-BT, V-LINK, Vgate, OBDLink LX/MX+. Not reachable from iOS unless MFi-certified; not reachable from a BLE-only client at all. Linux: `rfcomm bind 0 <mac> 1` -> /dev/rfcomm0.

known_limitations:
basic-clone tier (cloned firmware sold as "ELM327 v2.1"): legislated single-frame reads only. Multi-frame transmit, client-supplied flow control and sometimes ATCAF0 fail or are silently wrong. TuneECU Lite's own listing states clone v2.1 adapters do not work and a genuine v1.4/1.5 is required.
standards-elm327 tier: reliable for reads and custom headers, but multi-frame transmit and tight timing are firmware-dependent — this is the tier where maintenance functions become a coin toss.
advanced-stn tier (OBDLink LX/MX+/CX): adds dependable multiframe_tx, flow_control, raw_frames and the ST command set. This is what vendor tools name when a function must work.
native-can tier (SocketCAN, PCAN, Kvaser): adds monitor_all and non_standard_bitrate. No AT layer, so nothing is hidden — the research tier.
alt_can_bus (Ford MS-CAN, GM SW-CAN) cuts across the tiers: only the OBDLink MX, MX+ and EX provide it. An otherwise advanced-stn adapter without it cannot run FORScan's body and chassis module functions, because those buses sit on non-standard pins rather than behind a protocol setting.

models.name: UniCarScan UCSI-2100
models.notes: 255-byte message support is how it satisfies multiframe_tx. No SW-CAN/MS-CAN.

models.name: OBDLink MX Bluetooth
models.notes: SW-CAN and MS-CAN capable. Bluetooth Classic only — not reachable from iOS.

models.name: OBDLink MX+
models.notes: As MX, plus MFi so iOS works. The only wireless iOS adapter reaching MS-CAN/SW-CAN.

adapter_requirements: Single-frame reads (mode 01/03) work on essentially any adapter including clones.

Multi-frame ISO-TP transmit and custom request headers need sound firmware — an STN chipset (OBDLink LX/MX+/CX) in practice. This is the dividing line behind vendor tools accepting any adapter for reads while naming specific ones for maintenance functions.

requests.description: Mode 01 PID 00 — bitmask of supported live-data PIDs; a safe first liveness check.
requests.name: read_supported_pids

requests.description: Mode 03 — stored diagnostic trouble codes. Single frame, works on clones.
requests.name: read_dtcs

requests.description: Mode 09 PID 02 — VIN. Legislated, but the reply is multi-frame, which makes it the cheapest test of whether an adapter can reassemble ISO-TP at all.
requests.name: read_vin

requests.description: UDS ReadDataByIdentifier of the standard VIN DID — first step off the legislated path.
requests.name: read_vin_uds

can_formatting_off.description: ATCAF0 — raw frames; ISO-TP segmentation becomes the client's job. Clone firmware sometimes refuses.

echo_off.description: ATE0 — echo off; send before scripting anything.

flow_control_mode_1.description: ATFCSM1 — use client-supplied flow control. If this fails, multi-frame transmit will fail.

read_voltage.description: ATRV — adapter's estimate of battery voltage (approximate, not from the ECU).

reset.description: ATZ — full reset; returns the firmware banner. Claimed version is not proof of chipset.
